Soft water is a great thing to have. I live in a city in the Pacific Northwest and have extremely soft water too. A general rule of thumb is for lighter beers you'll need to add some acid to bring the pH down. In heavy roast beers you'll possibly need to add some bicarbonate (baking soda is easy) to bump the pH up a bit. Beyond that there's some personal preference; add sulfate for IPAs and chloride for maltier beers.

Strongly advise you not to add things willy-nilly though unless it's just basic things like a homebrewing forum thread (assuming you're doing all grain). If you don't have a good water profile and a brewing calculator, you can do more harm than good.

Personally, I have a ratcheting pulley and just lift the bag up and let it hang there to drip-dry. That way, I never have to deal with squeezing a hot, sticky bag. But if you want to squeeze, let it drain through a perforated bucket or something similar—just make sure you aren't leaving wort behind. You'd be surprised how much can remain in a bag, and how much that can hinder your efficiency. But crush is definitely key. I have an affordable grain mill, and it's been great. It easily paid for itself well within a year since I started buying sacks of base grain that come in about half the per-pound price from local homebrew shops.

Another tip is to hold back a gallon or two of water from your mash and do a cold water dunk sparge or something to coax out a few more percentage points. I don't bother with it since I don't have another large pot and my efficiencies are already good, but it's worth a shot if you want to try.
